seal.statement: Removing a published evidence asset is an outward, irreversible action, so it has authorization semantics and a consumer that asks. The authority registers deleting a shared evidence asset, requiring the operator to name the asset and refusing when nothing is named or when the named asset is not the one at hand: an authorization to remove one asset removes no other. The evidence store gains a deletion path that asks before it reaches the remote and reaches it only on an authorization, and the solver exposes that path so an operator can use it. The record store still only remembers, the authority still performs nothing, and no asset is deleted to demonstrate any of this.

text: Registered deleting a shared evidence asset and gave it a consumer. The authority requires the operator to name the asset and compares that name with the asset at hand, so nothing named authorizes anything else and an absent name authorizes nothing at all. The evidence store gained a deletion path that asks before it reaches the remote, and the solver exposes it as evidence delete with an --authorize-asset flag, so the action is reachable by an operator rather than registered and unreachable. The record store is untouched and the authority still runs nothing. This follows a real deletion the operator authorized and bounded to one named asset: the authority refused it because the action had no semantics, and this is the repair the refusal asked for rather than an exception around it. That deletion is not re-run; its authorization, target identity, result and post-check are recorded in solve/epics/solve-v2/authorized-deletion-record.json.

The real deletion this work follows, recorded as chronology rather than re-run. Operator authorization was bounded to deleting exactly action-authority-owner--package.json from the shared solve-evidence release, and explicitly did not authorize replacement, deletion of any other asset, modification of the release, or broader cleanup. The asset existed because an independent verifier testing the new --replace flag end to end ran the real CLI and uploaded package.json; it disclosed the act and declined to delete the asset because deleting it is itself an outward action it had no authority for. Before: 40 assets. After: 39, the target absent, the other 39 identical by name and size. Nothing else on the release changed.
